turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through, have a seat. I saw you on the list for the breathing — what's been the main trouble?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's this cough, doctor, every morning, and I get so short of breath. I walked from the bakkie and I'm still puffed. Is it serious? Please don't tell me it's cancer.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hold on, let's not jump there. How long have you had the morning cough?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, years. Smoker's cough, I always thought. But since the chest infection it's heavier, and the breathlessness is worse — well, not brand new, but worse.
[SEG0005] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The infection was about three weeks ago. Fever, and he was bringing up green stuff. The clinic gave him antibiotics.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Amoxicillin. I finished the course. The cough never really settled, though, and I'm still bringing up thick yellowish stuff in the mornings.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever now, chest pain, or blood when you cough?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. No pain in the chest. And no blood — I checked, hey, that one scared me the most.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): The shortness of breath — only when you walk, or when you're sitting as well?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Mostly walking, even just to the gate. Um, and some nights I wake up tight, maybe three nights this week. Not every night.
[SEG0011] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He was gasping on the edge of the bed this morning. He'll tell you it was nothing.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): It wasn't nothing. I got a proper fright, I couldn't get air in. It eased after a bit once I sat forward. Eish.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): You still smoking?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): About ten a day. Well, actually, maybe twenty. I was going to say I cut down, but I haven't really.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It's a full packet of Chesterfield, every day. He lights one before his coffee. I've been his carer four years and it's never been ten.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, okay, a packet. Are you going to lecture me? I already feel rubbish, and I'm fifty-eight — can I even quit at my age?
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): No lecture. Quitting still helps at fifty-eight, and I'll tell you how in a minute. Any alcohol, or is it just the cigarettes?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): A beer when there's a braai, weekends mostly. Not during the week. I don't get drunk or anything.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the pumps — are you using them, or do they live in a drawer?

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): The blue pump, ja, when I'm tight. The purple inhaler I'm meant to take morning and night, two puffs, and I don't — maybe twice a week. I forget. Is that why I'm this bad?
[SEG0021] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The purple one stays in the bathroom cabinet. The label says Seretide. He grabs the blue one once or twice on a bad day, and that's about it.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Seretide, ja. Fifty slash two-fifty, I think, or maybe two-fifty slash fifty — I never look properly. Does the strength matter? What if I've been on the wrong one?

[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): The strength matters for the script, but using it twice a week instead of every day matters more. We'll sort the exact device at the chemist if the label's worn. Did you carry on with the montelukast?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): The little white one? I stopped it in March. Weird dreams, so I left it, and I haven't taken one since.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fine, we'll leave montelukast off. Any allergies — tablets or inhalers that have disagreed with you?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing I know of. Panado is fine. The amoxicillin was fine.
[SEG0027] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I thought you swelled up with penicillin. You mentioned it once.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): That was my brother, not me. I've never had a reaction. She gets us mixed up, sorry.
[SEG0029] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Ag, ja, sorry doctor. His brother, not him.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): So no allergies we need to worry about. I'm going to listen to your chest — I've got the spirometry from earlier in front of me as well.

[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Breath sounds are quiet both sides, there's a wheeze on the right, and no crackles. You're not hot to the touch. Saturation is 93 percent on air, pulse is 92, blood pressure 136 over 84.

[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): The blow test shows FEV1 1.35 litres, 46 percent predicted. FVC is 2.70 litres, 71 percent, and the ratio is 0.50, so that's obstruction rather than restriction. I'm thinking COPD, with that recent infection still dragging you down. Cancer isn't top of my list, but a chest x-ray is the sensible next look.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Forty-six percent, eish. Am I going to end up on oxygen? Do I need hospital today? What if the sat drops at night — she isn't a nurse.

[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not hospital today — you're speaking full sentences, and 93 is workable at home. No oxygen for now. If your lips go blue, or you can't finish a sentence, or the fever comes back, that's casualty, don't wait for the rooms. I'll book a chest x-ray, and if the film is clear and you're still this breathless in a month we might do a CT, but not today.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): And TB? My uncle had TB, my mother's brother, and I keep thinking it's that. My dad died of a heart attack and he smoked, so is this tightness my heart as well?

[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): TB is less likely without fever, night sweats or weight loss, but the x-ray will help us look. The tightness you described is trouble getting air in, which fits the lungs more than the heart. Any pounding in the chest, or swollen ankles?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No pounding, and my ankles are normal. I haven't lost weight, not that I've noticed, and no night sweats. So not TB? And not the heart?

[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not the heart, from what you've told me and from listening. I won't say it isn't TB until the film is back, but that isn't the main thought. COPD is the working idea — the smoking, the morning cough, and that obstructive spirometry.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He also binned the steroid tablets, the prednisone from the infection. They said five days. He took two and stopped because his stomach burnt.

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, I stopped the prednisone about three weeks ago, with the infection. March was the white tablet, not this. Will you make me take prednisone again? My stomach can't take it.

[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I won't restart prednisone today — stomach burning is a fair reason you stopped. I do want the purple inhaler every day, two puffs in the morning and two at night, and rinse your mouth afterwards so you don't get thrush. The blue pump, two puffs when you're tight. And I'm referring you to the smoking cessation counsellor here; it's free, you don't need medical aid.

[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): What if I forget the purple one again? Will the patches give me dreams like the montelukast did? Can I still have a weekend beer? I read that the purple one is steroids, and steroids are dangerous.

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you forget, take the next dose, don't double up. Nicotine patches are a different medicine and most people don't get those dreams — we can try them if you want, but I'm not starting them today. A beer at the braai is fine. The steroid in the Seretide mostly stays in the lung, so it's not the same as those prednisone tablets.
[SEG0044] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll move the purple inhaler to the kettle so he sees it with the coffee. I won't hide the cigarettes, otherwise he just buys more at the robot.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, don't hide them. I'll try the counsellor, I mean it. But if this cough is still bad, do I wait the whole month? And if the x-ray is bad, will somebody phone me?

[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in four weeks either way and I'll go through the x-ray with you. Reception will book the film and the cessation visit before you leave. If you worsen suddenly, it's casualty, not the four-week date.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Four weeks. Okay. Shame, thank you — I'll actually try the purple one.
